One may also engineer in even greater constraints on the solution to Eq. 4, for example, by using external information (either manually or by applying an analysis based on contextual information) to group like voxels together, or as is described in Ref. [30], where the image space is initially assumed to be a single pixel/voxel. The example provided in Ref. [30] and shown as Fig. 5 demonstrates how ML-EM can over-fit SDF data relative to more constrained algorithm. The constrained algorithm was first presented in Ref. [30] and is called point-source likelihood (PSL). In PSL, a single source position and activity is inferred (forcing A in Eq. 4 to have a single non-zero entry = A /2). s In the simulated example shown in Fig. 5, the entire 5m×4m×6m space was voxelized to 10-cm LBNL Report #2001653 gridandtheactivitywithineachvoxelwasallowedtobenon-zero(ratherthanjustvoxelsidentified as occupied via SLAM, as is more typical). However, the example demonstrates how despite the Poisson loss being lower for the ML-EM solution, the PSL solution is much closer to the true input; placing the source position in the voxel below the true source position, rather than placing activity in most voxels with the highest activity near the trajectory. This example demonstrates how the ability to take prior information - in this case, that the non-background radioactivity is point-like - can produce significantly improved outcomes. Ref. [30] initially presented the PSL concept, but also considered the possibility that there is not just a single point-like source, but instead an unknown number of them. This latter possibility was presented alongside statistical tests to determine whether the addition of another set of free parameters is appropriate given the informationcontent ofthemeasurements.
